passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites. From each of their fathers’ tribes send one man who is a leader among them” (verse 2).

Moses sends them from the Wilderness of Paran. Twelve names follow, one from each tribe (verses 4-15). Among them are Caleb son of Jephunneh, from Judah, and Hoshea son of Nun, from Ephraim. The list ends with a note: Moses gave Hoshea the name Joshua (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Israel has reached the edge of the promise. It is more than a year since the exodus. The people are camped near Kadesh, just south of Canaan. The land God swore to give to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lies ahead.

Notice how God describes the land before a single scout sets out. It is the land ‘which I am giving to the Israelites’. The mission is not to find out whether the land can be taken. That has been settled by God's word. The scouts are sent to see what kind of land it is and to bring back a report.

Deuteronomy adds that the people first asked for scouts and Moses agreed (Deuteronomy 1:22-23). Numbers presents the mission as commanded by God. Many readers take the two together: the people asked, and God allowed it.

The twelve are leaders, but they are not the twelve tribal chiefs of chapters 1 and 2. They are different men. Only two of the names will matter.

One of those names is changed. Hoshea means salvation. Moses renames him Yehoshua, Joshua, which means the LORD saves. The change puts God's own name into the man's name. Before the scouts leave, the reader is told where rescue will come from.
passages.later:
In Greek the name Joshua is Iesous, the name given to Mary's son: ‘you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins’ (Matthew 1:21).

Hebrews notes that Joshua, who later led Israel into the land, could not give the people their final rest: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8).
passages.asks: God called the land his gift to Israel before anyone had seen it. Ask what God has said about your future that you treat as an open question. And ask whether you look into a hard thing in order to obey, or in order to find a reason not to.

passages.happening:
Moses gives the scouts their instructions. “See what the land is like and whether its people are strong or weak, few or many” (verse 18). Are the towns open camps or fortified? Is the soil rich or poor? “Be courageous, and bring back some of the fruit of the land” (verse 20). It is the season of the first ripe grapes.

They travel the length of the land, from the Wilderness of Zin in the south to Rehob in the far north (verse 21). They come to Hebron, where the descendants of Anak live (verse 22). In the Valley of Eshcol they cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carry it on a pole, and they take pomegranates and figs (verse 23).

“After forty days the men returned from spying out the land” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Moses' questions come in pairs: strong or weak, few or many, good or bad, camps or fortresses. They are sensible questions. Nothing in the chapter suggests that it was wrong to look.

The season of the first grapes falls in late summer in the hill country. The valley was named Eshcol, which means cluster, after the grapes cut there. The picture of two men carrying one cluster on a pole has become a lasting image of the land's richness. For people who had eaten manna in a desert for over a year, the fruit was proof they could hold in their hands.

Hebron is mentioned with a note about its age: it was built seven years before Zoan, a city in the Nile delta. The note stresses how old and settled the town was. But a first hearer would have known Hebron for another reason. Abraham had lived there. He, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob were buried there, in the one plot of Canaan that Abraham had ever owned. The scouts stand beside the graves of the people who received the promise.

Kadesh, the base they return to, is usually placed at the springs of Ain el-Qudeirat and Ain Qadeis in the northeast of the Sinai Peninsula.

The forty days will matter. In the next chapter God will name one year in the wilderness for each of them.
passages.later:
Genesis tells how Abraham bought the burial cave near Hebron: “So the field and its cave were deeded by the Hittites to Abraham as a burial site” (Genesis 23:20).

Hebron comes back at the end of the story. Decades later Caleb, by then an old man, asked for this very hill country as his share, and he drove out the three clans of Anak named here (Joshua 15:14).
passages.asks: The scouts carried back fruit they had not grown, from a land they did not yet hold. Ask what foretaste of God's goodness you have already been given. And ask whether it has made you more willing to trust him for the rest.

passages.happening:
The scouts report to Moses, Aaron and the whole congregation at Kadesh, and show the fruit. “We went into the land to which you sent us, and indeed, it is flowing with milk and honey. Here is some of its fruit!” (verse 27).

Then the report turns. “Nevertheless, the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified. We even saw the descendants of Anak there” (verse 28).

“Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, ‘We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!’” (verse 30). “But the men who had gone up with him replied, ‘We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!’” (verse 31).

They spread a bad report: the land ‘devours its inhabitants’, and its people are giants. “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, and we must have seemed the same to them!” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
All twelve scouts agree about the facts. The land is good. It is ‘flowing with milk and honey’, the Bible's usual phrase for a rich land: milk from flocks on good pasture, and honey, which may mean bees' honey or a thick syrup made from dates. The fruit is there for all to see. Everything God said about the land has turned out to be true.

They also agree that the people are strong and the towns walled. That was true too. Archaeology has shown that many Canaanite cities of that age had massive walls and earth ramparts.

The whole report turns on one word: ‘Nevertheless’. The ten and the two saw the same land and the same walls. They differ over one thing only, whether God can be trusted to give what he has promised.

Watch how the ten scouts' words grow as they speak. First the people are ‘stronger than we are’. Then the land itself ‘devours its inhabitants’, though they are holding its fruit. Then everyone they saw was huge. Then they saw the Nephilim, the mighty men named in Genesis from before the flood. Fear feeds on its own words.

The Hebrew word for their ‘bad report’ usually means slander, damaging talk spread about a person. Here it is spread about the land, and so about the God who promised it.

Their last sentence is the most revealing. ‘We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight.’ They had measured themselves against the enemy and left God out of the measuring. Then they assumed the enemy saw them the same way. They could not have known that. It was their own fear speaking. Years later a woman of Jericho would tell Israel's spies that the people of the land had in fact been melting in fear of Israel all along (Joshua 2:9-11).

Caleb's answer is one short sentence. He does not deny the walls. He simply says, ‘We must go up.’

The chapter stops there, with the people's answer still to come.
passages.later:
Moses remembered the people's words: “Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying: ‘The people are larger and taller than we are; the cities are large, with walls up to the heavens’” (Deuteronomy 1:28).

Rahab of Jericho later told the other side of the story: “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us” (Joshua 2:9).

Hebrews gives the reason the generation failed: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:19). Hebrews writes this as a warning to the church about its own heart, not as a charge against anyone else.
passages.hard:
The Nephilim lived before the flood (Genesis 6:4). How could the scouts have seen them in Canaan?

Readers answer in several ways. Many point out who is speaking. The claim comes from the scouts whose report the text itself calls bad. They were frightened, and they reached for a name out of legend to make the sons of Anak sound unbeatable. The chapter records what they said. It does not say they were right.

Others think ‘Nephilim’ had become a general word for people of unusual size, without any claim that they descended from the figures of Genesis 6. Genesis 6:4 itself says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days ‘and afterward as well’, which some take to reach beyond the flood. Those who read the flood as a regional event have a further option. The notes on Genesis 6 set out how that passage is read.

Whichever answer is preferred, the chapter's own point is plain. The report was shaped by fear. Caleb saw the same people and was not afraid, and in the end it was Caleb who drove the sons of Anak out of Hebron (Joshua 15:14).
passages.asks: The ten scouts measured themselves against the walls and left God out. Ask what problem looks so large to you that you feel like a grasshopper beside it. And ask whose report you have been believing about it: Caleb's, or the ten's.
